gem_identification.note: The defense of retaliatory eviction was first established in Wisconsin by common law in Dickhut v. Norton. The defense was subsequently codified by the legislature in Wis. Stat. § 704.45, and Paulik v. Coombs is the leading case interpreting that statute.

currency_gemini.limitation_scope: The common-law defense of retaliatory eviction established in Dickhut was superseded by the legislative enactment of Wis. Stat. § 704.45. In Paulik v. Coombs, the Wisconsin Court of Appeals explicitly held that this comprehensive statute now provides the exclusive remedy for retaliatory evictions in Wisconsin, thereby superseding the Dickhut common-law defense. While the public policy principles from Dickhut were codified, the specific judicial test and common-law cause of action are no longer the governing authority.
currency_gemini.note: Although the specific common-law defense created by Dickhut has been superseded by statute, the case remains historically significant for first establishing the legal principle of a retaliatory eviction defense in Wisconsin, which the legislature subsequently adopted and codified.

currency_gemini.note: Paulik v. Coombs established the controlling burden-shifting framework for adjudicating claims of retaliatory eviction under Wis. Stat. § 704.45. A review of subsequent Wisconsin case law and statutory amendments reveals no authority that has overruled, abrogated, or significantly limited this holding. The framework requires the tenant to first establish a prima facie case, after which the burden of production shifts to the landlord to offer a legitimate, non-retaliatory reason for the eviction. The ultimate burden of persuasion then rests with the tenant to prove the landlord's proffered reason is pretextual. This case continues to be cited as the standard for this analysis in Wisconsin.

Ann. § 1-21-1211, which prohibits landlords from increasing rent, decreasing services, or seeking possession because a tenant has made good faith complaints about code violations or has joined a tenants' union. There is no significant body of case law from the Wyoming Supreme Court establishing or interpreting this statutory defense in the residential context.
